constraints: Ordering is not a business invariant.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Standard queues simplify scaling but transfer ordering and duplicate handling to the application.
details.errorCorrection: Duplicates alone do not require FIFO, S3 is not a queue, and network security groups do not define message ordering.
details.mechanismOrProperty: SQS Standard queues are designed for high throughput and at-least-once delivery. FIFO queues address ordering and deduplication constraints with different throughput behavior.
details.scenarioApplication: The owner selects Standard, records a message identifier, and makes the business operation idempotent before scaling consumers.

messages.text: FIFO is for ordering and deduplication requirements; duplicates in a Standard queue are handled by idempotent consumers.
S3 objects do not provide queue delivery, acknowledgement, and consumer semantics.
Network path behavior does not define SQS message order.

feedback.reason: Standard queues favor scale and throughput with at-least-once delivery, so consumers must handle duplicates and possible reordering.

options.text: Evaluate an SQS Standard queue for its high-throughput, at-least-once delivery model, and make the consumer idempotent.
Use FIFO because FIFO is required for every workload that can receive duplicate messages.
Use an S3 bucket because S3 object order provides queue delivery semantics to consumers.
Use a security group because network ordering determines the order in which SQS consumers receive messages.

prompt: A workload needs very high throughput and can tolerate occasional reordering, while each message must be processed at least once. Which SQS queue type should be evaluated?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Fine-grained groups improve concurrency but require a correct ordering key and careful handling of hot partitions.
details.errorCorrection: One global group serializes all messages, Standard queues do not provide FIFO group ordering, and one queue per message is unnecessary.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Messages with the same MessageGroupId are processed in order, while messages in different groups can be processed concurrently subject to queue and consumer limits.
details.scenarioApplication: The producer uses a stable customer key, and the team monitors hot groups that can serialize one customer’s traffic.

messages.text: A single group creates one serialization boundary and prevents the desired per-customer concurrency.
Standard queues do not provide the FIFO message-group guarantee.
A message group is an ordering key, not a reason to create a queue per message.

feedback.reason: FIFO message groups define the ordering boundary and permit parallel progress across independent groups.

options.text: Use one FIFO message group ID per customer or ordering key so messages within a group stay ordered while different groups can progress independently.
Use one message group for the entire queue because FIFO queues always process all messages concurrently.
Use a Standard queue and sort messages after processing because SQS FIFO group IDs are only network labels.
Use one queue per message because message groups cannot express ordering boundaries.

prompt: Orders for each customer must remain ordered, but different customers should be processed concurrently. How should an SQS FIFO queue be partitioned?

constraints: The logical message has a stable identity.
The consumer still handles duplicates defensively.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Queue deduplication reduces duplicate enqueues but is time-bounded and not a substitute for end-to-end idempotency.
details.errorCorrection: Random IDs defeat deduplication, security groups do not inspect message identity, and disabling retries loses messages after ambiguous failures.
details.mechanismOrProperty: SQS FIFO uses deduplication IDs or content-based deduplication within its deduplication interval. A producer timeout does not prove whether the first send succeeded.
details.scenarioApplication: The producer reuses the order event ID on retry, and the consumer records processed IDs to handle retries outside the FIFO deduplication window.

messages.text: A different ID on each retry tells SQS that the messages are different.
Network controls do not deduplicate application messages.
A timeout leaves the send result ambiguous, so retries and idempotent handling are required.

feedback.reason: FIFO deduplication depends on a stable logical message identity or supported content-based behavior; application idempotency remains necessary.

options.text: Use a stable MessageDeduplicationId for each logical message or the supported content-based deduplication behavior, and keep the consumer idempotent.
Use a random deduplication ID on every retry because different IDs cause SQS to recognize the messages as the same order.
Use a security group rule because network retries are deduplicated before they enter the FIFO queue.
Disable retries because FIFO queues guarantee that a timed-out producer request was never accepted.

prompt: A producer may retry SendMessage after a timeout and must avoid enqueueing the same logical order twice within the FIFO deduplication interval. Which design should be used?

constraints: The consumer must delete only after success.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Long visibility can delay retries after a crashed worker, so the value should balance processing time and failure detection.
details.errorCorrection: Deleting before success loses work, zero timeout increases duplicate concurrency, and network timeouts do not define SQS visibility.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A message becomes visible again when the timeout expires unless deleted. A longer timeout reduces concurrent duplicate processing but does not eliminate failures or duplicates.
details.scenarioApplication: The consumer sets a safe baseline, uses ChangeMessageVisibility for long work, and retries or sends a failed message to a DLQ.

messages.text: Deleting before work succeeds can lose the message permanently.
A zero timeout makes messages immediately visible and increases duplicate processing.
SQS visibility is a queue property and not a security-group TCP timeout.

feedback.reason: Visibility timeout hides a received message temporarily; it must cover processing or be extended, and the message should be deleted only after successful work.

options.text: Set the queue visibility timeout above the expected processing time and extend it for long-running messages when needed, while retaining idempotent processing and deleting only after success.
Delete the message immediately after ReceiveMessage because visibility timeout guarantees processing success.
Set visibility timeout to zero so all consumers can process every message concurrently without duplicates.
Use a security group timeout because SQS visibility is determined by TCP connection state.

prompt: A consumer usually finishes in 20 seconds but sometimes needs 90 seconds. Messages are reappearing while the first consumer is still working. What should be changed?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A low receive threshold moves transient failures too quickly; a high threshold delays isolation, so it should reflect retry behavior and processing cost.
details.errorCorrection: An indefinite visibility timeout hides rather than isolates poison messages, deletion destroys evidence, and S3 lifecycle does not manage SQS messages.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The redrive policy moves messages after repeated receives according to maxReceiveCount. The DLQ has its own retention and access policy and is not a discard sink.
details.scenarioApplication: Operations alerts on DLQ depth, inspects the message and error, fixes the consumer, and replays safely with idempotency.

messages.text: Increasing visibility can delay retry but does not diagnose or isolate a message that will never succeed.
Deleting failed messages loses diagnostic evidence and may lose business events.
S3 lifecycle rules do not move SQS messages to a DLQ.

feedback.reason: A dead-letter queue isolates messages that exceed the receive threshold so the main queue can continue and operators can investigate.

options.text: Configure a dead-letter queue with an appropriate maxReceiveCount, monitor it, and redrive messages only after the failure cause is fixed and the replay impact is understood.
Increase visibility timeout indefinitely because a poison message will eventually succeed without operator intervention.
Delete every failed message immediately because a DLQ prevents debugging and cannot preserve message bodies.
Use an S3 lifecycle rule because lifecycle expiration automatically moves failed SQS messages to a diagnostic queue.

prompt: A consumer repeatedly fails on malformed payment messages and blocks useful work. Which SQS pattern should isolate the failed messages?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Controlled redrive takes longer but limits overload and duplicate business effects.
details.errorCorrection: A DLQ does not guarantee replay safety, deleting loses events, and visibility timeout does not make redrive transactional.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Redrive moves messages back to a source or destination queue; it does not undo side effects from prior attempts or guarantee safe replay.
details.scenarioApplication: Operations samples and validates messages, replays gradually, and tracks success, duplicate outcomes, and residual failures.

messages.text: A DLQ identifies repeated failures but does not make all messages safe for concurrent replay.
Deleting the DLQ destroys the failed messages and is not a recovery strategy.
Visibility timeout controls redelivery timing and does not provide transactionality.

feedback.reason: DLQ redrive is a recovery operation that must account for message correctness, side effects, capacity, and duplicate processing.

options.text: Inspect and validate the DLQ messages, redrive them at a controlled rate or to a staging queue first, monitor side effects, and rely on idempotent consumers.
Redrive all messages at once because a DLQ guarantees that every message is safe to replay concurrently.
Delete the DLQ because redrive is unsafe and the original producer can recreate only the failed messages automatically.
Change the queue visibility timeout to zero because zero visibility makes redrive transactional.

prompt: After correcting a consumer bug, the team needs to replay DLQ messages without flooding the production queue. Which operational approach is safest?

constraints: The workload can wait for messages.
The consumer should reduce API calls.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Long polling reduces empty requests but can hold connections and requires client timeout and concurrency tuning.
details.errorCorrection: Short polling increases empty responses, security groups do not control SQS receive behavior, and S3 listing is not queue consumption.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Long polling uses a receive wait time and should be coordinated with the client HTTP timeout. It does not make delivery exactly once or eliminate the need for retries.
details.scenarioApplication: The consumer configures queue or receive-level wait, handles timeout and retry behavior, and measures empty receives and message latency.

messages.text: Zero-wait polling increases empty responses and API calls.
Network idle settings do not control SQS long-polling semantics.
S3 listing does not provide message visibility, acknowledgement, or queue delivery.

feedback.reason: SQS long polling waits briefly for messages and can reduce empty receives and associated API calls.

options.text: Use SQS long polling with a suitable WaitTimeSeconds value and align the consumer HTTP timeout so it exceeds the wait.
Poll continuously with a zero-second wait because empty responses are cheaper than waiting on SQS.
Use a security group idle timeout because network idle state controls whether SQS returns an empty response.
Move messages to S3 because S3 listing is a lower-cost substitute for SQS long polling.

prompt: A consumer polls an often-empty SQS queue and incurs many empty ReceiveMessage responses. Which change reduces unnecessary polling?

constraints: The queue account owns the resource policy.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Cross-account policy coordination adds maintenance but prevents producer compromise from becoming consumer or queue administration access.
details.errorCorrection: sqs:* is broader than needed, security groups do not authorize SQS APIs, and public queues violate the trust boundary.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The queue policy grants resource-side access while the producer identity policy grants the caller’s action. SQS actions are separable for send, receive, delete, and attribute access.
details.scenarioApplication: Security tests sending and denied receiving from the producer role and keeps the consumer permissions in a separate account or role.

messages.text: The producer needs SendMessage, not every queue action.
SQS cross-account authorization is policy based and not controlled by security groups.
Public queue access is unsafe and unnecessary for a known cross-account producer.

feedback.reason: Cross-account SQS access requires compatible identity and resource policies, and the producer should receive only the action it needs.

options.text: Use a queue resource policy and producer identity policy that allow only SendMessage for the approved principal and queue ARN, leaving receive and delete permissions to the consumer role.
Grant the producer account sqs:* because cross-account queues require every action on both sides to succeed.
Use a security group to authorize SendMessage because SQS queue policies cannot name a principal from another account.
Make the queue public so the producer can send without a cross-account policy handshake.

prompt: A producer in one AWS account must send messages to a queue in another account, but it must not receive or delete messages. Which policy design is appropriate?

constraints: Producers and consumers have different roles.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Customer managed keys improve ownership and auditability but add policy, cost, and key-availability dependencies to the queue path.
details.errorCorrection: Scoped key permissions are supported, security groups do not authorize KMS, and endpoint TLS does not replace at-rest encryption with the customer key.
details.mechanismOrProperty: SQS uses the configured KMS key for server-side encryption. Key policy, IAM permissions, grants, and queue policy must permit the required operations.
details.scenarioApplication: Security tests sending and receiving with the intended roles, denies administration to workloads, and monitors KMS access and key lifecycle.

messages.text: Workloads should receive only the KMS actions needed for their queue path, not kms:*.
KMS authorization uses key and IAM policies rather than security-group membership.
TLS protects the connection and does not satisfy the stated customer-managed at-rest encryption design.

feedback.reason: SSE-KMS adds KMS key-policy and IAM dependencies to SQS message operations, which must be scoped to the service and required roles.

options.text: Configure SSE-KMS with the selected key and grant the SQS service and required producer or consumer roles only the key actions needed for encrypted send and receive operations.
Grant kms:* to every producer and consumer because encrypted SQS messages cannot be used with scoped KMS permissions.
Use a security group on the KMS key because encryption authorization follows the queue subnet.
Disable queue encryption because TLS on the SQS endpoint makes stored messages encrypted at rest automatically for the customer key requirement.

prompt: A queue contains sensitive messages and must use a customer managed KMS key with least-privilege producer and consumer access. Which dependency should be configured?

constraints: Failures must return messages for retry.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Managed polling reduces infrastructure but batch size, concurrency, and retry behavior can amplify failures if not tuned.
details.errorCorrection: Custom polling is unnecessary for the standard integration, S3 notifications are a different event path, and deleting before invocation loses failed messages.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Lambda polls SQS through the event source mapping, passes batches to the function, and deletes messages after successful processing according to the integration model.
details.scenarioApplication: The owner tunes batch size and visibility timeout, configures a DLQ or failure destination, and tests partial and full batch failures.

messages.text: Lambda event source mappings provide the managed SQS polling integration.
S3 notifications do not replace the SQS-to-Lambda event source mapping.
Messages must remain available for retry until processing succeeds; early deletion can lose work.

feedback.reason: An SQS event source mapping lets Lambda poll the queue and invoke the function in batches, with retry behavior tied to function success or failure.

options.text: Configure an event source mapping from SQS to Lambda with batch size, visibility timeout, concurrency, and failure handling aligned to the function’s processing time.
Have the Lambda function poll the queue from every invocation because event source mappings cannot integrate with SQS.
Use S3 notifications because S3 automatically polls SQS and invokes Lambda with queue visibility semantics.
Delete messages before invoking Lambda because the event source mapping guarantees successful function execution.

prompt: A Lambda function should process messages from an SQS queue without a custom polling fleet. Which integration should be configured?

constraints: The function can identify failed records.
The queue has a DLQ policy.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Partial responses improve throughput and reduce duplicate work but require precise handler reporting and per-record error isolation.
details.errorCorrection: A whole-batch error retries successful work unnecessarily, deleting first loses failures, and security groups do not select message failures.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The Lambda handler returns batch item failures, allowing successful messages to be deleted while failed records remain available for retry according to the event-source behavior.
details.scenarioApplication: The function validates each record, records idempotency before side effects, and sends poison records to the DLQ after the configured receive threshold.

messages.text: A whole-batch error causes successful records to be retried and does not isolate the two invalid messages.
Deleting before validation loses failed records and does not send them to the DLQ.
Message failure reporting is part of the event source contract and not a network rule.

feedback.reason: Partial batch responses allow the event source to retry only failed SQS records when the function reports their identifiers.

options.text: Enable SQS event-source partial batch response behavior and return the failed message identifiers, while keeping each successful operation idempotent.
Return one function error for every batch because Lambda always deletes successful records before the handler returns.
Delete all 10 messages in the handler before validating them because the DLQ stores failed records automatically after deletion.
Use a security group rule to mark two message IDs failed because event-source failure selection is a network control.

prompt: A Lambda batch contains 10 messages and only two are invalid. The team wants successful messages deleted while the invalid ones retry or reach the DLQ. Which behavior should be enabled?

constraints: The operation has an external side effect.
The message has a stable business identifier.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Idempotency state adds storage and cleanup work but is required for safe at-least-once processing with side effects.
details.errorCorrection: Visibility timeout only delays redelivery, FIFO does not control an external provider, and early deletion can lose the payment event.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A consumer can crash after charging and before deleting, so a redelivery is possible. A durable idempotency record or provider idempotency key makes repeated attempts safe.
details.scenarioApplication: The consumer checks and records the order ID atomically with the business state, then deletes the message after successful processing.

messages.text: Visibility timeout does not make the external payment operation exactly once.
FIFO controls queue ordering and deduplication, not the behavior of an external payment provider after a crash.
SQS deletion is not a distributed transaction with the payment provider.

feedback.reason: SQS delivery and the external side effect are not one transaction; idempotency must be enforced at the business-operation boundary.

options.text: Use an idempotency key or deduplication record for the business operation, apply the side effect conditionally, and delete the SQS message only after the result is durable.
Assume visibility timeout provides exactly-once payment execution and skip all idempotency state.
Use FIFO ordering alone because FIFO guarantees that an external payment provider will never receive a duplicate request.
Delete the message before charging because SQS deletion makes an external operation transactional.

prompt: A Standard queue may redeliver a payment message after a consumer timeout. Which application design prevents a duplicate charge?

constraints: The producer knows the delay at send time.
Consumers should not poll hidden work as visible work.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Delay can simplify scheduled handoff but is bounded and not a substitute for a durable workflow scheduler when timing or state is complex.
details.errorCorrection: Visibility timeout is post-receive, DLQs isolate failures, and IAM policies do not schedule message delivery.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A per-message delay can defer one message; a queue delay can apply a default to messages. Visibility timeout hides a message after a consumer receives it.
details.scenarioApplication: The producer selects the appropriate delay scope and the team tests that delayed messages do not enter consumer processing prematurely.

messages.text: Visibility timeout starts after receipt and does not defer the first delivery.
A DLQ is for failed messages and does not schedule normal work.
IAM policy conditions authorize actions and do not schedule message visibility.

feedback.reason: SQS message timers delay a message before it becomes available, while visibility timeout applies after a receive.

options.text: Use an SQS message timer or supported per-message delay, and distinguish it from the queue-wide DelaySeconds setting and visibility timeout.
Use visibility timeout because visibility timeout delays a message before its first receive even when it has never been consumed.
Use a DLQ because DLQs delay every message until its business start time.
Use an IAM policy condition because policy evaluation schedules message visibility for a future timestamp.

prompt: A workflow should not make a message visible to consumers until five minutes after it is produced. Which SQS feature matches the requirement?

constraints: The maximum outage window is known.
Messages expire after the business retention period.
The DLQ has its own recovery policy.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Long retention improves outage recovery but costs more and can retain sensitive or stale events beyond their usefulness.
details.errorCorrection: Visibility timeout does not extend retention indefinitely, CloudTrail does not contain message bodies, and indefinite retention creates uncontrolled cost and data exposure.
details.mechanismOrProperty: SQS deletes messages when the retention period expires, whether or not a consumer successfully processed them. The DLQ is a separate queue with retention behavior.
details.scenarioApplication: The owner models outage and investigation time, sets source and DLQ retention, and alerts before messages approach expiration.

messages.text: A short retention window can expire messages during the outage; visibility timeout does not override retention.
CloudTrail records API calls and does not reconstruct expired message bodies.
Indefinite retention is not automatically appropriate and increases cost and governance burden.

feedback.reason: Queue retention determines how long unconsumed or failed messages remain available and must cover the recovery and replay objective.

options.text: Set the SQS message retention period longer than the maximum expected outage and replay window, then align the source and DLQ retention policies with the business requirement.
Set retention to one minute because visibility timeout keeps messages forever when consumers are unavailable.
Use CloudTrail retention because CloudTrail can reconstruct the message body after SQS expires it.
Disable retention expiration because all event queues should retain messages forever regardless of business value.

prompt: A consumer outage may last two days and messages must remain available for recovery, but the queue should not retain events indefinitely. Which setting should be designed?

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More retries improve resilience to transient errors but increase latency, cost, and duplicate side effects before isolation.
details.errorCorrection: Zero can discard transient failures too quickly, unlimited retries can block or duplicate work, and route metrics do not count SQS receives.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The redrive policy moves a message after it has been received unsuccessfully enough times. The value should reflect failure modes and the visibility timeout.
details.scenarioApplication: The service owner tests transient and permanent failures, alerts on DLQ depth, and keeps replay idempotent.

messages.text: Moving every first failure immediately can discard messages during a temporary downstream outage.
Unlimited retries can delay isolation and amplify duplicate processing.
SQS counts message receives through queue semantics, not route-table hops.

feedback.reason: maxReceiveCount balances transient retry opportunity against poison-message isolation.

options.text: Set the redrive policy’s maxReceiveCount based on the expected transient retry window and processing cost, then monitor the DLQ for poison messages.
Set maxReceiveCount to zero because the first failed receive should always move the message to the DLQ.
Set maxReceiveCount to unlimited because retries never increase duplicate side effects when SQS is used.
Use a route table metric because SQS counts receive attempts from network hops rather than consumer receives.

prompt: A transient downstream outage should allow retries, but a permanently malformed message should move to a DLQ after a bounded number of attempts. Which setting controls the boundary?

constraints: The error is deterministic for that payload.
The original payload is needed for repair.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Isolation adds operational triage but protects queue availability and preserves the failed event for repair.
details.errorCorrection: More workers do not fix deterministic input, zero retention discards evidence, and deleting the queue destroys healthy messages.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A DLQ and redrive policy bound repeated delivery. Concurrency alone multiplies failed attempts and can consume capacity without fixing the payload.
details.scenarioApplication: Operations preserves the original message, identifies the schema or code defect, fixes the consumer, and replays through a controlled path.

messages.text: Concurrency increases failed attempts and does not change a deterministic malformed payload.
Immediate expiration loses the event and diagnostic evidence rather than isolating it safely.
A single poison message does not justify deleting healthy queued work.

feedback.reason: A deterministic malformed message is a poison message and should be isolated so healthy work can progress while the payload remains available for diagnosis.

options.text: Treat the message as a poison message, use a DLQ and bounded receive policy to isolate it, and repair or replay it after the consumer and payload are understood.
Increase consumer concurrency without a DLQ because more workers will make a deterministic malformed message valid.
Reduce queue retention to zero because expiration is the only way to stop one failed message from being delivered again.
Delete the entire queue because any poison message means the queue cannot preserve healthy events.

prompt: A malformed message causes every consumer to fail repeatedly, and the queue backlog grows. Which diagnosis and mitigation is correct?

constraints: The service has a latency objective.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Age-based scaling improves latency response but can create more workers than the downstream can handle without a capacity limit.
details.errorCorrection: Queue length does not account for variable processing or message age, security groups are unrelated, and rising age calls for scale-out or diagnosis rather than scale-down.
details.mechanismOrProperty: ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage is a service metric that reflects how long the oldest available message has waited. Scaling must still respect downstream capacity and visibility behavior.
details.scenarioApplication: The owner combines age with backlog, concurrency, and error metrics and tests scale-out before downstream saturation.

messages.text: Queue length alone can hide age and processing-time differences.
Security-group rule count is not an SQS backlog or age metric.
A rising oldest-message age indicates increasing delay and is not evidence that consumers are catching up.

feedback.reason: The age of the oldest message directly indicates queueing delay and can reveal missed latency objectives better than count alone.

options.text: Scale using ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage together with backlog and worker-capacity signals, then validate that added concurrency does not overload the downstream service.
Scale only from queue length because one message always takes the same time and age is unrelated to latency.
Scale from security-group rule count because network rules directly represent the age of an SQS message.
Scale down when the oldest message age rises because an older message means consumers are catching up.

prompt: A queue-backed worker fleet scales from the total message count, but the count fluctuates and old messages still miss their processing deadline. Which metric is a better scaling signal?

constraints: The database has a hard concurrency limit.
Messages must eventually be retried or processed.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A cap can increase backlog and latency during bursts, but it preserves downstream availability and allows controlled recovery.
details.errorCorrection: Unbounded concurrency can overload the database, moving normal burst traffic to a DLQ loses the intended flow, and unlimited connection attempts amplify failure.
details.mechanismOrProperty: SQS can support many consumers, but event-source or worker concurrency and database connection pools determine pressure on downstream systems. A DLQ is for failed messages, not normal burst shedding.
details.scenarioApplication: The owner sets a concurrency ceiling, tests burst recovery, and alerts when oldest-message age rises or database throttling appears.

messages.text: SQS does not guarantee that a downstream database can accept unlimited concurrent work.
A DLQ isolates repeated failures and is not the normal capacity-control mechanism for healthy bursts.
Unlimited connection attempts can exhaust the database and do not make processing connectionless.

feedback.reason: Queue throughput must be bounded by the slowest downstream dependency, with explicit retry and backlog monitoring.

options.text: Cap worker or Lambda event-source concurrency at a safe database level, use visibility and retry settings that match processing time, and monitor age, errors, and throttling.
Remove all concurrency limits because SQS guarantees that downstream services will accept every parallel consumer request.
Use a DLQ as the primary capacity limiter and move every message there during a burst before attempting normal processing.
Increase database connection attempts without limit because queue consumers never hold connections during message processing.

prompt: A queue backlog grows during a burst, but the downstream database supports only 20 concurrent writes. Which worker design protects the database while draining the queue?
